newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian-Japanese quietly celebrate new freedom.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian-Japanese quietly celebrate new freedom.

text.p: A lone Christmas tree greeted the latest batch of Peruvian-Japanese hostages to be freed from the siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence by Marxist guerrillas.

"It's just so nice to be out. When I saw the Christmas decorations here, I just felt overwhelmed," said Cesar Morisaki, one of the 57 Peruvian hostages of Japanese descent who gathered with their relatives at Lima's Peruvian-Japanese Society after their release on Sunday night.

"The worst thing was the lack of any information, and not knowing from hour to hour what might be going on outside, what sort of negotiations might be being done," said Lucho Sakode, 47. "But we were all happy that our wives had been freed first and that at least they were okay. That kept me going."

His wife, released on Tuesday night along with about 80 other women, was among the group of ladies in matching floral print aprons who had organised the gathering, modestly decorated with a nativity scene made of paper.
On the bulletin board was a paper and ink sign listing the 57 names of the Peruvian-Japanese hostages that were freed late on Sunday night.

The mood was one of quiet rejoicing, with many of the former captives and their relatives blinking at the camera flashes and swarming reporters, mostly from Tokyo, and graciously offering their comments, many in halting Japanese.
The modesty of the event contrasted sharply with the general mayhem outside the besieged residence, where hundreds cheered and clapped as the hostages were driven out in buses.

Though freed, Peruvians of Japanese descent still seemed to carry the burden of knowing that most Japanese nationals were still captive, and that their days in the spotlight from this incident were far from over.
There were few tears of joy or raised voices but many embraces and kissing. In one corner, a few couples silently held each other, their eyes closed.

The low-key atmosphere was enlivened briefly by the arrival of former first lady Susana Higuchi, who breezed into the dimly-lit conference hall with television cameras, reporters and bodyguards in tow.

Higuchi had earlier told reporters that her former husband President Alberto Fujimori was concerned about his brother Pedro Fujimori, who was among the 140 remaining hostages along with Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki and most of the up to 60 Japanese nationals, including government staff and businessmen.
Both Fujimori and Higuchi are children of Japanese immigrants to Peru.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), who stormed and seized the Japanese ambassador's residence during a party last Tuesday, released 225 of the around 340 hostages late on Sunday.

Asked whether he supported Fujimori's tough stance towards the MRTA, demanding that they lay down their weapons before negotiations can start in earnest, freed hostage Juan Takao said, "If his brother was not still in there, it would be a lot different. Because he is willing to be tough even though he has family in there, I respect it."
